raw_case_text:
A 2 months old child admitted in the month of May, 2018 into the children emergency room, of the University of Calabar Teaching Hospital with complaints of cough of one-month duration and fever of three weeks duration. Cough was distressing and worse at night. Fever was high grade, intermittent and temporarily relieved by administration of paracetamol syrup. Pregnancy was booked at a gestational age of 13 weeks. Delivery was at a gestational age of 28 weeks via emergency lower section caesarean section. Birth weight was 1.65kg. Child was admitted into special care baby unit and managed for prematurity, neonatal sepsis and neonatal jaundice on account of antepartum haemorrhage. She had blood transfusion but no exchange blood transfusion and was discharged at a weight of 1.8kg having spent a month in special care baby unit. Child was fed with infant formula and breast milk from birth. She is the second child in a monogamous setting and has a 7-year-old male sibling. The father is a civil servant while the mother is a businesswoman.
Physical examination showed an acutely ill looking child, febrile with temperature of 38.6 C, mildly pale, dyspnoeic and tachypnoeic, with a weight of 3.7kg (3rd percentile), length of 50cm (below the 3rd percentile) and occipito frontal circumference - 38cm (z-score). Respiratory rate was 66cycles/minute, with SPO2 of 80% in room air. The heart rate was 186 beats/minutes with normal heart sounds. The abdomen had a tender hepatomegaly of 6cm and a splenomegaly of 6cm. Liver was 8cm below the right costal margin, soft and smooth. Spleen was 2cm below the left costal margin, and non-tender.
Laboratory findings showed a PCV of 21%, random blood sugar of 4.7mmol/L, HIV screening was negative, Full blood count; Total WBC of 12.6 x 109/L, Neutrophils: 65%, Lymphocytes: 33%, Platelets: 179x109/L, Malaria parasite test: positive, Gene Xpert: negative, Mantoux test: 0 mm, Chest X-ray showed hazy opacities on the right upper and middle lung lobes, with left upper lobar opacities and pneumatoceles (Figure 1). Blood culture yielded T. ptyseos. Patient was on oxygen at 2L/min and was transfused with 60mls of settled cells. Post transfusion PCV was 25%. While on admission, patient received IV Ceftriaxone and IV gentamicin and spent 5 days during which fever subsided and respiratory rate reduced, and was thereafter discharged. One week later, patient represented and was admitted on account of the same but worsening symptoms. A diagnosis of Septicaemia with heart failure was made to rule out bronchopulmonary dysplasia and pulmonary tuberculosis. Empirical antibiotic (IV Ceftriaxone, IV Gentamicin, Suspension Azithromax) therapy were commenced. IV Furosemide and tablets digoxin was also given. On the second day of admission, IV cloxacillin was commenced, as the child remained ill and IV gentamicin discontinued. 3 days into admission, child developed seizures which was generalized tonic clonic lasting about 1-2 minutes. She had two episodes. The second episode was aborted with IV diazepam. The random blood sugar at the time was 2.9mmol/L. SPO2 was 67%. Intravenous fluid was commenced at 60% maintenance and phenobarbitone was also commenced at maintenance dose. She received blood transfusion, Nil per oral and cautious intravenous fluid, and oxygen therapy. Frusemide and digoxin were also added. Despite these measures, she was still very ill and in severe respiratory distress. CSF analysis was not in keeping with meningitis. She remained very ill, had intermittent hypothermia with subnormal temperature and died 5 days after admission. Blood culture result of sample taken on the third day of admission and received 3 days after patient s demise yielded growth of T. ptyseos. Antimicrobial susceptibility test result showed sensitivity to Amikacin, intermediate to Ceftazidime and Ciprofloxacin, and resistant to Ceftriaxone, Cefuroxime, Gentamicin, Amoxicillin-Clavulanate, Cefepime, Cefoxitin and Colistin.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-month-old preterm-born female infant presented in Calabar, Nigeria, with a 1-month history of distressing nocturnal cough and a 3-week history of intermittent high-grade fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born at 28 weeks' gestation (spending 1 month in the special care baby unit), the 2-month-old infant presented in May 2018 with 4 weeks of distressing nocturnal cough and 3 weeks of paracetamol-responsive intermittent high fever. After partial improvement during a 5-day admission, she was readmitted 1 week later with worsening respiratory distress, congestive heart failure, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
subjective.past_medical_history: Delivered at 28 weeks' gestation via emergency cesarean section for antepartum hemorrhage (birth weight 1.65 kg); hospitalized for 1 month in the SCBU for prematurity, neonatal sepsis, and neonatal jaundice requiring blood transfusion; mixed-fed with breast milk and infant formula.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for distressing cough, intermittent high fever, dyspnea, and during readmission generalized tonic-clonic convulsions.

objective.physical_examination: Acutely ill, febrile (38.6 C, later developing intermittent hypothermia), mildly pale, dyspneic, and tachypneic (RR 66 cpm), SpO2 80% on room air (dropping to 67% during readmission seizures), HR 186 bpm, weight 3.7 kg (3rd percentile), length 50 cm (<3rd percentile), OFC 38 cm. Abdomen showed tender hepatomegaly (6 cm; 8 cm below right costal margin) and non-tender splenomegaly (6 cm; 2 cm below left costal margin).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: PCV 21% (25% post-transfusion), WBC 12.6 x 10^9/L (65% neutrophils, 33% lymphocytes), platelets 179 x 10^9/L, random blood sugar 4.7 mmol/L (dropping to 2.9 mmol/L during readmission seizures), and negative HIV screen, GeneXpert, and Mantoux test (0 mm). Chest X-ray showed right upper/middle lobe and left upper lobe hazy opacities with pneumatoceles.
objective.advanced_workup: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis on readmission excluded meningitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal multidrug-resistant Tatumella ptyseos septicemia and necrotizing pneumonia (with pneumatoceles and heart failure) co-existing with malaria in a 2-month-old former 28-week preterm infant. Malaria parasite test was positive, and blood cultures from both admissions grew Tatumella ptyseos (sensitive only to amikacin, intermediate to ceftazidime/ciprofloxacin, and resistant to ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, gentamicin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefepime, cefoxitin, and colistin). Treated with packed-cell transfusions, oxygen, IV ceftriaxone, gentamicin, azithromycin, cloxacillin, furosemide, digoxin, diazepam, and phenobarbitone, but died on day 5 of readmission before the second culture sensitivity report returned.
